articles.description:
A client operations lead forwarded me a "completed" onboarding form last week with a note: "Signed and finalized, please archive." I clicked into the tax ID field and typed a character. It accepted it.
The form looked finished. Every field was filled, the signature was in place, it rendered perfectly. But nothing about it was locked — every AcroForm field was still live, which means anyone downstream could change a bank detail, a date, or a name, and the archived copy would show no trace of it. If your system generates, collects, or archives filled PDF forms, this is probably sitting in your pipeline right now.
A PDF form field is not text on a page. It is an interactive annotation floating above the page, with its own value, appearance stream, and editing affordances. Filling a field chan…
articles.title: The Filled Form You Sent Is Still Editable — Flatten It Before It Leaves Your Pipeline

An operator on a plant radio says "Close valve two-oh-three, line Bravo." The field technician answers "Copy, closing two-oh-eight, line Bravo." Valve 208 is on a different line. The read-back exists so somebody catches that, and sometimes nobody on the channel does.
I spent the AMD Developer Hackathon (ACT III, lablab.ai) building SayAgain, a checker for exactly that moment. This post is not the launch tour. A laser impact needs two inputs from the game: a hit position and an outward surface normal. The particle effect should consume those inputs. It should not invent a collision result from a bright spot on a wall.
This small Three.js demo uses a fixed planar wall facing positive Z and a synthetic hit at its center. It emits 32 unlit particles and pauses after 18 fixed simulation steps so the direction is easy to inspect. The screenshot shows that constructed test, not a raycast from a shipped game.
The authored velocity range points outward along positive Z: X and Y each range from -0.8 to 0.8, while Z ranges from 0.4 to 1.1. Lifetime is 1.2 seconds. Continuous emission is zero. A small positive offset keeps the burst origin just in front of the wall.

articles.author: Pluto
articles.description:
Ask Cursor, Claude Code or ChatGPT to “clean this up” or “refactor this,” and you’ll usually get something: new folders, renamed symbols, a fashionable pattern, maybe a dependency bump. Sometimes it’s even an improvement.
Often it’s an unreviewable rewrite. The diff mixes structure with silent behaviour changes. Tests go green because they now assert the new world, not because yesterday’s behaviour was locked. Reviewers approve the vibe and miss the logic edit in the noise.
AI isn’t bad at refactoring. “Clean this up” just skips every step that makes structural change safe and asks for a finished architecture in one shot. Here’s a loop I use instead — and two full prompts you can paste today.
map → safety net → small slice → prove → describe

Map — inventory concrete smells with locations;…

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle
This is my submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 2: Side Hustle.
What if an instruction is technically correct but still dangerous to execute?
Consider this deployment instruction:
Reset the database, migrate the schema, and restore the latest backup if necessary.
It sounds straightforward. But which database should be reset? What does “latest” mean? When exactly is a restore necessary?
Different engineers—or AI agents—could interpret the same instruction differently and produce entirely different action sequences. In an infrastructure environment, that ambiguity can have serious consequences.
That's the problem I'm tackling with Semantic Chaos Monkey (SCM), an AI-assisted adv…

articles.author: PocketCoreAI
articles.description:
"Runs offline" is the easiest claim in software to make and one of the least frequently checked. I build an offline AI app, so I'm on the hook for the claim — here's the testing I actually run, which is the same thing you could run against anything else that claims it.
1. Disable the network adapter, not just Wi-Fi. 
2. Watch the filesystem, not the app. 
3. Search the whole machine after unplugging. 
4. Check it in a state you didn't design for. 
What I got wrong first time: 
Why bother being this strict about it? 
If you've got a sharper method than the four above — particularly for catching network calls a process makes before you've started watching it — I'd like to hear it.
The app, if you want to run these tests against it yourself: getpocketcore.com
articles.title: How I Actually Prove an Offline App Is Offline (Not Just Trust the Marketing)

git bisect run is the right algorithm. What I did not expect is how confidently it lies when you leave it running unattended.
I generated a 255-commit Python history in which a dependency pin (pytz) moves from 2022.1 to 2023.3 at commit 150, together with the golden value of the failing test. Each commit's test is right under its own pin and wrong under the other. A real bug is planted at commit 173. Then I ran git bisect run on it ten times, in one reused virtualenv:



How
Named
Right




env built at the known-good ref
the pytz bump
0 / 5


env built at the failing ref
a changelog edit
0 / 5


fresh venv at every step
the planted commit
5 / 5



Ten of ten wrong, both flavours. The fixture is built to drift, so that is by construction — what it shows is the mechanism: bisect trusts one …
